Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is a gastrointestinal motility disorder that results from the reflux of stomach contents into the esophagus or oral cavity resulting in symptoms or complications. The typical symptoms of GERD are heartburn and regurgitation of gastric contents into the oropharynx. GERD affects quality of life and may cause erosive esophagitis, esophageal strictures, and Barrett esophagus, a precursor to esophageal adenocarcinoma. GERD is a clinical diagnosis and is most effectively treated with proton-pump inhibitors (PPIs). Long-term use of PPIs is associated with bone fractures, chronic renal disease, acute renal disease, community-acquired pneumonia, and Clostridium difficile intestinal infection.

Gastroesophageal reflux (GER) in children is very common and refers to the involuntary passage of gastric contents into the esophagus. This is often physiological and managed conservatively. In contrast, GER disease (GERD) is a less common pathologic process causing troublesome symptoms, which may need medical management. Apart from abnormal transient relaxations of the lower esophageal sphincter, other factors that play a role in the pathogenesis of GERD include defects in esophageal mucosal defense, impaired esophageal and gastric motility and clearance, as well as anatomical defects of the lower esophageal reflux barrier such as hiatal hernia. The clinical manifestations of GERD in young children are varied and nonspecific prompting the necessity for careful diagnostic evaluation. Management should be targeted to the underlying aetiopathogenesis and to limit complications of GERD. The following review focuses on up-to-date information regarding of the pathogenesis, diagnostic evaluation and management of GERD in children.

Symptoms potentially attributable to gastroesophageal reflux disease are among those most commonly reported to primary care providers in the outpatient setting. In this review, we discuss clinical approaches to the evaluation and management of these symptoms, including proton pump inhibitor trials as well as specific indications or clinical settings that warrant referral to Gastroenterology specialists.

data.narrative: Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is a gastrointestinal motility disorder caused by reflux of stomach contents into the esophagus or oral cavity, producing symptoms or complications [18#0]. The disease entity is documented across multiple normalized records and literature concepts [1][2][3][6][9][15], and the concept Gastroesophageal Reflux appears as a recognized literature entity [3]. The characteristic symptoms of GERD are heartburn and regurgitation of gastric contents into the oropharynx [18#1]. Symptoms potentially attributable to GERD are among those most frequently reported by patients in primary care outpatient settings [20#2]. In children, clinical manifestations are varied and nonspecific, necessitating careful diagnostic evaluation [19#3]. In the pediatric population, gastroesophageal reflux is often physiological and managed conservatively, whereas GERD represents a less common pathologic process causing troublesome symptoms [19#4]. A review of GERD in children is published as PMID 36170502 [11] under the title Gastroesophageal reflux disease in children: What's new right now? [12]. GERD may cause erosive esophagitis, esophageal strictures, and Barrett esophagus, which is a precursor to esophageal adenocarcinoma [18#5]. Pathogenic factors include abnormal transient relaxations of the lower esophageal sphincter, defects in esophageal mucosal defense, impaired esophageal and gastric motility and clearance, and anatomical defects of the lower esophageal reflux barrier such as hiatal hernia [19#6]. Long-term use of proton-pump inhibitors is associated with bone fractures, chronic renal disease, acute renal disease, community-acquired pneumonia, and Clostridium difficile intestinal infection [18#7]. GERD is a clinical diagnosis most effectively treated with proton-pump inhibitors [18#8]. Management approaches include proton pump inhibitor trials and specific indications warranting referral to gastroenterology specialists [20#9]. Multiple clinical trials address GERD treatment, including a famotidine trial in non-erosive GERD [4], a pantoprazole efficacy trial in patients with acid reflux symptoms [7], an on-demand treatment study [13], and a placebo-controlled study of endoscopic fundoplication [16]. Additional PubMed records on GERD are identified as PMID 29132520 [5], PMID 33351044 [8], PMID 37034973 [14], and PMID 37516506 [17]. A natural history study of gastroesophageal reflux in children and adolescents is also registered [10].
